stories.headline: Fantasy football matchup rankings for Week 1: Mayfield, Hampton in great spot
stories.summary: The most- and least-favorable matchups in the NFL for this week's games at the four key fantasy positions: QB, RB, WR and TE.
stories.body:
Making tough lineup decisions each week can be the most challenging part of the fantasy football process. When you're torn between two similar players and simply don't know which to start, start the player with the superior matchup.

Ah, but exactly how does one determine the best (and worst) weekly matchups?

Week 1 is the toughest week as far as evaluating matchups. It's commonplace for fantasy analysis to rely heavily upon the previous year's statistics, even though that completely ignores how quickly and dramatically this game changes, especially over a seven-month offseason.

Our matchup rankings provide a schedule-independent method to evaluate positional matchups each week, ranking all 32 opposing defenses in order of most to least favorable for opposing players at all four skill positions (quarterback, running back, wide receiver and tight end). Instead of relying upon seasonal totals, we calibrate points-allowed data to show how each defense fared relative to the difficulty of the schedule it has faced. This provides a fairer approach to judging the quality of individual matchups.

For the first three weeks, these rankings account for two things: my own opinion of the strength of that matchup, and what ESPN's projections tell us about it. As an additional reference point, 2025 full-season data is provided.

"Adj. FPA," or adjusted fantasy points allowed, reflects how far above or below players' weekly PPR fantasy point averages that defense held opponents at that position. A positive number means that the matchup is favorable; a negative number means it is unfavorable. Also, remember teams often use multiple running backs and wide receivers in a game, and these plus/minus averages cover all of a team's personnel at that position.

Finally, one caveat: Matchups are only one ingredient in my rankings formula. Not every favorable matchup should be exploited, nor unfavorable matchup avoided. If you want my -- and the ESPN fantasy staff's -- most complete source for whom to start and sit each week, consult our weekly rankings.

Quarterbacks
Matchups highlight: Baker Mayfield, Tampa Bay Buccaneers (at Cincinnati Bengals). Mayfield draws an all-around outstanding fantasy matchup, facing a weaker defense in a game with a projected pass-friendly game flow, as Buccaneers-Bengals began Week 1 with the highest over/under. The Bengals finished 2025 the sixth-most-favorable matchup for quarterbacks, and while they added DTs Jonathan Allen and Dexter Lawrence and DE Boye Mafe during the offseason, they still have a long way to go to straighten out a unit that posted the league's worst pass rush win rate. Mayfield is a high-end superflex/QB2 with top-10 positional scoring potential for Week 1.

Others to like: Justin Herbert, Los Angeles Chargers (vs. Arizona Cardinals); Kyler Murray, Minnesota Vikings (vs. Green Bay Packers).

Matchup to avoid: Patrick Mahomes, Kansas City Chiefs (vs. Denver Broncos). Credit Mahomes for working hard to get himself back into the lineup in time for Week 1, nine months to the date when he tore both the ACL and LCL in his left knee in a Week 15 game last season. Nevertheless, he's unlikely to display the level of mobility he did pre-injury, at least in the early weeks, and he faces one of his worst matchups all season in his first game back. Only five times in 2025 did the Broncos afford a quarterback more than 15 fantasy points in a game, and they return largely the same defense this year, with the most prominent exception the departure of DE John Franklin-Myers.

Running backs
Matchups highlight: Omarion Hampton, Chargers (vs. Cardinals). He's in a situation conducive to a major breakthrough, with limited competition behind him in the banged-up Keaton Mitchell and Kimani Vidal, and a running-back-friendly offensive coordinator in Mike McDaniel. Hampton should see a massive workload in this home game, which featured the week's widest opening spread (-10), while facing a defense that was the fourth-worst against the position in 2025. The Cardinals allowed 11 games of 15-plus fantasy points to running backs last season, and five of those came in the final six weeks alone.

Others to like: Breece Hall, New York Jets (at Tennessee Titans); Kenny Gainwell, Buccaneers (at Bengals); Mike Washington Jr., Las Vegas Raiders (vs. Miami Dolphins).

Matchup to avoid: MarShawn Lloyd, Packers (at Vikings). There's a lot to like about Lloyd's season-long fantasy prospects following Josh Jacobs' placement on the commissioner exempt list, and unsurprisingly, over the past month, no player improved more in terms of ADP than the 25-year-old speedster (up from the undrafted pool and into the 10th round). That said, Lloyd is no guarantee to see the level of usage we've come to expect from a typical feature back, and Chris Brooks appears likely to handle a good amount of three-down work. Considering this matchup, against a Vikings defense that allowed only six games of 15-plus fantasy points to the position in all of 2025, it's best to leave this backfield to the fantasy sidelines for future evaluation.

Wide receivers
Matchups highlight: Tetairoa McMillan, Carolina Panthers (vs. Chicago Bears). He was one of last season's more underrated wide receivers, the No. 16 scorer at his position despite playing for what was the league's sixth-worst offense. McMillan now kicks off his sophomore year facing a defense that, despite boasting a two-time Pro Bowl cornerback in Jaylon Johnson, struggled mightily against opposing wide receivers last season. Teams' No. 1 wide receivers on the whole averaged nearly three full fantasy points more against the Bears in 2025 than they did in a typical week, and 11 of them (in 18 games) scored 17 or more in those contests.

Others to like: DeVonta Smith, Philadelphia Eagles (vs. Washington Commanders); Ladd McConkey, Chargers (vs. Cardinals); Tre Tucker, Raiders (vs. Dolphins).

Matchup to avoid: Terry McLaurin, Commanders (at Eagles). I'm as big a believer in a McLaurin rebound as anyone, but Week 1 doesn't seem like the time for him to begin formulating his case. He has a shaky history lining up across from Eagles All-Pro CB Quinyon Mitchell, averaging only 10.4 fantasy points and 4.8 targets in their four career games against one another (including the 2024 NFC Championship Game). Additionally, the Eagles added CB Riq Woolen to strengthen their secondary during the offseason, giving them one of the league's strongest top threes at the position when including slot CB Cooper DeJean.

Tight ends
Matchups highlight: Dallas Goedert, Eagles (vs. Commanders). The Eagles' passing game matches up brilliantly on all fronts against a bad Commanders defense, but Goedert could be a particularly big factor in this contest. Projected No. 2 wide receiver Makai Lemon missed a good amount of the preseason with a hamstring issue, and his depth-chart listing as the team's primary punt returner hints he might have a limited role in the offense initially, shifting more of the focus to the tight end. Between Goedert (Week 16) and Grant Calcaterra (Week 18), Eagles starting tight ends totaled 22.3 fantasy points in their two 2025 meetings with the Commanders, who didn't improve their secondary substantially during the offseason.

Matchup to avoid: Dalton Kincaid, Bills (at Texans). The Texans allowed more than 13 fantasy points to tight ends in only three games last season, and all three of them were by elite, name-brand players: Trey McBride, Brock Bowers and George Kittle. Kincaid's talent might be in the ballpark of that group, but his usage is a far cry from theirs. He averaged 4.17 targets per game in 2025, a number exceeded by 23 other tight ends who played in at least half their teams' games.

stories.headline: Cleveland Cavaliers offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: After missing out on an epic homecoming with LeBron James, our insiders examine what to expect from the Cavaliers in the 2026-2027 season.
stories.body:
The Cavaliers quietly retooled much of their roster beyond their core four -- Donovan Mitchell, whom they signed to a four-year, $273M extension; James Harden, whom they signed to a new three-year $97M deal; Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen.

They lost longtime guard Max Strus and forward Dean Wade but traded for 3-and-D wing Peyton Watson, who the team hopes can shore up a porous perimeter defense and signed a four-year, $88M contract.

After losing in the first round in 2022-23, the second round in 2023-24 and 2024-25, and then the conference finals last season, the next step is obvious for the Cavaliers and their core. The question is: Do they have the personnel to make it?

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season, with 30 previews -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Cavaliers coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: Peyton Watson, Mario Hezonja

Key subtractions: Dean Wade, Dennis Schroder, Max Strus, Larry Nance Jr., Keon Ellis

Key retentions: Donovan Mitchell, James Harden

The Cavs' failed pursuit of LeBron James this summer turned into a pivot for a younger, athletic wing, prying Watson from the Nuggets after a career year.

Watson averaged career highs in points, rebounds, assists and steals while shooting 41% from 3 last year, and he has in recent years been one of the strongest wing defenders in the league. That makes him a strong complement next to James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, as the Cavs hope he can provide a substantial answer to the elusive fifth starter role next to their core four. -- Jamal Collier

Zach Kram's offseason grade: B

The Cavaliers' offseason effectively boiled down to the Peyton Watson sign-and-trade, as they dealt a bunch of their 2025-26 depth -- most notably Max Strus -- for the ability to fit Watson onto their cap sheet. They also re-signed James Harden to a new three-year deal, which might not age well but helped them escape the second apron.

Those are risky but necessary moves for a team that wants to win now; the the 23-year-old Watson increases Cleveland's championship upside due to his potential as an athletic 3-and-D wing. -- Kram

What we learned over the past few months
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: Donovan Mitchell won the summer.

Cleveland was in the middle of the action this summer with LeBron James weighing another homecoming to Ohio and giving James Harden a new three-year deal. Given those developments, it might be easy to overlook the fact that Mitchell signed a four-year, $273 million contract extension. That's an enormous amount of cash.

Mitchell, 29, is firmly in his prime, earning All-NBA second team honors and finishing seventh in MVP voting last season. And even though Cleveland was swept out of the playoffs by the New York Knicks, Mitchell did reach the conference finals for the first time in his nine-year career.

But the size of Mitchell's new contract probably deserves more scrutiny than it has received. The seven-time All-Star is set to earn more than $60 million in 2027-28. By comparison, Knicks guard Jalen Brunson, a more accomplished player, will earn $40.5 million.

Mitchell is currently on pace to be a top-10 earner once his new extension kicks in, but his deal will run through his age-34 season. Shouldn't his $75.5 million player option for the 2030-31 season make the Cavaliers a little squeamish?

If Mitchell were a better defender or an elite playmaker for his teammates, these numbers might be easier to stomach. As it stands, Cleveland's decision to pay him top dollar feels a bit ominous. -- Golliver

The big question: How will the team benefit from a full season from James Harden?
During Cleveland's run to the Eastern Conference Finals last year, it was easy to forget the team had dramatically reshaped its roster just a few months earlier, adding Harden to the mix at the deadline in February.

Harden reiterated several times during the postseason that he was learning on the fly, so he will presumably benefit from having a full offseason and camp.

The Cavs hope it will result in added pick-and-roll chemistry with their bigs, smoother symmetry with Mitchell and more productive bench units with him running the show. -- Collier

Post-free agency Power Rankings: Cavaliers are 8
Summer Forecast: Projecting Cleveland's 2026-27

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 11
Here are the predicted Net Points per 100 possessions for the Cavs' top seven players for the 2026-27 season.

As a rule of thumb, defenses should aim to stop the opponent's best player, as opposed to stopping the supporting cast.

But now the Cavs have two players who play dramatically better in wins versus losses.

Harden is 7.5 net points better in wins than losses (fourth-biggest change) and Mitchell is 6.5 better (13th), implying that stopping both is important and a more difficult challenge for defenses. -- Dean Oliver

Read about how Net Points works here.

Biggest X factor
G Jaylon Tyson

With Max Strus, Dean Wade, Keon Ellis and Dennis Schroder all departing over the summer and only Peyton Watson arriving as an external replacement, the Cavaliers will be relying on more internal help to backfill their production on the wing.

Tyson should be the second man up behind Watson, after he averaged a strong 13.2 points in 26.9 minutes per game in his sophomore season, while making 45% of his 3s.

Tyson fell to the fringes of the rotation in the playoffs, however, where he averaged only 4.1 points in 12.7 minutes per game. The former first-round pick needs to improve his consistency and reliability in big games, but in theory, his 3-and-D abilities would make him a perfect role player amid Cleveland's star-studded lineup. -- Kram

Betting insight from our expert
Bet to make ahead of the season: Cavaliers to qualify for conference semifinals (+125); to win Central Division (+195)

The Cavaliers were the top seed in the Eastern Conference two seasons ago after winning 64 games with a plus-9.5 PPG scoring margin.

Last season, after a down regular season due in part by injuries to point guard Darius Garland, the Cavaliers rode the late-season trade of Garland for James Harden and played their way to the Eastern Conference Finals.

While the Eastern Conference as a whole got stronger this offseason, the Cavaliers should return a team with the same key players who have demonstrated the capacity for success in both the regular season and playoffs.

To be able to bet them -- at plus money -- to make it a round earlier than they made it last season, is good value, even in the new Eastern Conference. -- André Snellings

stories.headline: Premier League panel: Harry Maguire goal vs. Ipswich right to stand, Arsenal deserved penalty vs. Aston Villa
stories.summary: The Premier League's Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel has said the decision to allow a Man United goal against Ipswich after an apparent handball by Maguire was correct and added that VAR should have intervened to award Arsenal a penalty against Villa.
stories.body:
The Premier League's Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel has said the decision to allow a Manchester United goal against Ipswich after an apparent handball by Harry Maguire was correct and added that VAR should have intervened to award Arsenal a penalty against Aston Villa.

The ball appeared to come off Maguire's hand as he controlled it just outside the penalty area during the match on Aug. 30. He then unleashed a shot, which was going wide before being deflected in by Jacob Greaves in United's 5-2 win.

The handball was deemed to be accidental by both referee Craig Pawson and VAR Jarred Gillett, and because Maguire's shot did not go in directly, that meant the goal was allowed to stand.

The KMI Panel is an independent group comprised of three former players or coaches, one Premier League representative and one from Pro Ref. Panel findings on key incidents in every game-week are being published this season for the first time.

The Panel notes on this incident, published on Wednesday morning, said: "Maguire's arms are within his bodyline, meaning that the contact with his right arm was accidental and not a punishable handball offence given that Maguire was not the goal scorer.

"The shot was clearly off-target and then deflected in via the defender for a clear own goal. The panel supported the referee's call to award the goal, 4:1, with one panellist considering the handball to be deliberate."

On the day of the match, the Premier League's Match Centre account on X posted: "The referee's call of goal for Manchester United was checked and confirmed by VAR - with it deemed that Maguire was not the immediate goalscorer after an accidental handball."

The same post also quoted the VAR: "It's an own goal and the accidental handball is not punishable, so we recommend you award the goal."

Elsewhere, the panel felt VAR should have intervened to award Arsenal a penalty in their match at Aston Villa on Aug. 31 for a challenge by Ian Maatsen on Bruno Guimarães. No foul was given but the panel unanimously felt it should have been, either on-field or after review.

- Marcus Rashford returns to training ahead of Manchester United's Champions League clash

- Premier League VAR review: Should Forest's goal have stood vs. Spurs?

"Clear contact was made on the attacker's standing leg and Maatsen made no contact with the ball," the panel notes read.

"They also felt that VAR should have intervened as the non-penalty award was a clear and obvious error."

The panel also felt the "reckless" challenge by Maatsen was worthy of a second caution.

The panel also disagreed three to two with the decision to award Nottingham Forest a penalty at Liverpool for a challenge by goalkeeper Alisson Becker on Neco Williams in the match on Aug. 29, but believed VAR was right not to overturn it because it did not meet the threshold of a clear and obvious error.

The panel also disagreed 4-1 with the on-field decision not to award Brentford a penalty at Leeds on the same day for Jayden Bogle's challenge on Kevin Schade, but again felt it did not meet the threshold of a clear and obvious error which would require VAR to overturn it.

Overall, the panel identified 21 KMIs in the second match round, with 76% dealt with correctly on-field in its view. That percentage rose to 90 after VAR interventions.

stories.headline: Max Verstappen admits to McLaren, Mercedes talks before 'following heart' with Red Bull stay
stories.summary: Max Verstappen has admitted to serious talks with McLaren and Mercedes before agreeing his Red Bull extension last month.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen has admitted to serious talks with McLaren and Mercedes before agreeing his Red Bull extension last month.

Verstappen ended a long period of uncertainty about his future with the new Red Bull deal, announced ahead of his home race, the Dutch Grand Prix, which overwrote a deal lasting until 2028 with one running through to the end of 2030.

The existence of escape clauses in his old deal had allowed rumours of moves elsewhere to spread.

Verstappen has acknowledged that he explored options with rival teams before committing to a longer deal.

"Of course, any kind of chat you take seriously," Verstappen said in a BBC Sport interview when asked about how serious talks were with McLaren and Mercedes. "They're all very respectful chats. There's nothing wrong with that."

Verstappen has been with Red Bull for his entire Formula 1 career. The company signed him to a developmental deal in 2014 before handing him a debut with junior team Toro Rosso the following season.

He memorably won for Red Bull on his first appearance with the team after replacing Daniil Kvyat at the 2016 Spanish Grand Prix.

He spent five seasons at the team before winning his first championship in 2021, the first of four consecutive titles.

- Spanish Grand Prix: Everything you need to know about the Madring

- Red Bull sign Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11

- Leclerc advice for Max vs. 100 drivers: Don't crash!

Verstappen pointed out he could have left Red Bull in those fallow years and ultimately opted to stay this time around as he believes Red Bull can be contenders again in future.

"I felt that staying was, for me, the right choice," he said. "You have to follow your heart. I could have run away very early on in my Red Bull career and gone somewhere else to try and win. If you have a little bit of patience, you do end up winning. I feel like that's my approach now as well."

Part of the uncertainty around Verstappen's future had been linked to his discontent with Formula 1's controversial new hybrid engines, which have shifted a lot of emphasis onto energy management and deployment.

Verstappen has labelled this "anti-racing" and likened the new F1 to Mario Kart.

F1 is making tweaks to the engines in 2027 and 2028 to lessen the importance of the electrical elements and Verstappen hopes this will lead to an improvement in how the racing feels.

"Hoping that it will be better in the future," he said. "Accepting where we are at the moment. Still the love for the sport. Not at the moment the driving. But the love for the sport.

"I love competition, naturally. I just hope that in the coming years, towards 2030, it can only get better. And to start to make the best of it, because these are the rules for the next four or five years."

stories.headline: Fantasy baseball news and notes: Diamondbacks get pitching help and more for Wednesday
stories.summary: All of the important fantasy spin and actionable takeaways resulting from the latest baseball news.
stories.body:
Everything that happens in and around MLB has some additional context when viewed from a fantasy baseball perspective. From lineup changes to minor league call-ups to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values in fantasy baseball.

Our fantasy baseball buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around MLB.

Sept. 9: Wednesday's news to know
By Todd Zola

Today marks the third consecutive day with an array of afternoon affairs. The action gets underway at 1:10 p.m. ET with the Detroit Tigers hosting the Minnesota Twins. Four more matinees follow, leaving 10 evening contests.

A pair of injured pitchers are set to return from the IL and tag-team today's game between the Arizona Diamondbacks and Kansas City Royals. The Diamondbacks enter the game one half-game ahead of the San Diego Padres for the third NL wild-card spot. Zac Gallen and Michael Soroka will take the hill after both missed an extended absence. Gallen was sidelined for almost two months due to right elbow inflammation, while Soroka was shelved for over two weeks as a result of right shoulder inflammation. Neither is stretched out for a regular workload, but both can handle three or four innings.
Last night, Jac Caglianone was out for his second straight game -- and he may not play tonight against the Diamondbacks. The sophomore slugger is dealing with a left flexor strain. The Royals will try to avoid being swept tonight, then have tomorrow off.
Gunnar Henderson left last night's game in the eighth inning after fouling a ball off his shin. He stayed in the game and coaxed a walk, but after hustling to second on a groundout, the trainer came out to check on him and they left the field together. Henderson is set for imaging in advance of tonight's tilt between the Baltimore Orioles and Cleveland Guardians at Camden Yards.
The Guardians have played the last four games without Chase DeLauter as he's been nursing a sprained right wrist. The club is optimistic that he can avoid an IL visit, but they may keep him sidelined for tonight's rubber game with the Orioles, hoping that DeLauter can return on Friday after the club's off day tomorrow.
Aaron Judge was 0-for-3 with two strikeouts in last night's return to the New York Yankees lineup. The club wants to ease him back into things, so they removed him in the seventh with the club holding a slim 2-1 lead over the Colorado Rockies. Judge was replaced by Heliot Ramos, who hit a three-run homer in the eighth, which proved to be the difference in the Yankees' 5-3 win. Manager Aaron Boone indicated that Judge would continue to be lifted early and occasionally get a maintenance day off.

Be sure to check out the latest fantasy lineup advice as well as the MLB betting tips for Wednesday.

Sept. 8: Yankees activate Judge

By Tristan H. Cockcroft

Exactly 99 days after his last appearance for the team, No. 99 -- Aaron Judge -- was activated by the New York Yankees on Monday night. He'll rejoin the lineup for their series opener against the Colorado Rockies at Yankee Stadium on Tuesday night.

Fantasy managers will instinctually race to get Judge back into their lineups with this news and, considering your likely alternatives in the outfield, it's a logical move. But those in ESPN standard leagues should take advantage of the daily lineup flexibility, as we probably won't see full-strength, or full-usage, Judge over the next few days.

Yankees manager Aaron Boone indicated over the weekend that Judge, who wasn't sent on a minor league rehab assignment prior to activation, might still require a ramping-up process as he works himself back to full strength. "Maybe it's playing a game, having an off day," Boone told The Athletic's Chris Kirschner. "Maybe it is playing 5, 6, 7 innings in a game and get him out. Those things are on the table."

Considering the lengthy absence and the fact that Judge resumed hitting only about three weeks ago, it's expected that he'll likely need workload management, otherwise he might struggle to recapture full form if he's immediately restored into an everyday role. Frequent starts as a DH, early exits from games (particularly blowouts in either direction) and days off might be the norm over at least the next week. This is where the ESPN standard league format grants Judge's managers an advantage, as those willing to monitor the Yankees' daily lineup release will know which days he's starting and, therefore, worth using.

One advantage Judge gains is that the visiting Rockies have some of the weakest pitching in baseball, their staff ERA a major league-worst 5.47 (and a third-worst 5.09 ERA if only counting road games). During this series, they're scheduled to start Gabriel Hughes, Tomoyuki Sugano and Ryan Feltner, pitchers who combined have a 5.64 ERA, 1.45 WHIP, 15.8% strikeout rate and average of one home run allowed per 22.5 at-bats. Judge is also 7-for-9 with three homers against Sugano in his career.

Judge would be a clear fantasy starter for any of those games he starts, even with the prospect of early exits, and that these favorable matchups come this quickly in his return only helps us evaluate him for tougher, later-September assignments. Figure that Judge will make two starts in the Rockies series and probably put forth quality hitting stats, but he might struggle more against tougher New York Mets pitching -- Nolan McLean on Friday represents the toughest upcoming Judge matchup -- and therefore be an iffier call for that three-game series.

Expect closer to full-form Judge in roughly 10 days -- which is good timing, consider it would align him for a potentially full-force version of himself right in time for head-to-head championship matchups in ESPN leagues.

Todd Zola's other news to know for Tuesday

All 15 Tuesday games will be played under the lights. Action commences at 6:35 p.m. ET when the Cleveland Guardians visit the Baltimore Orioles.
Riley Cornelio is set to start tonight's game for the Washington Nationals when they visit the San Diego Padres. Cornelio has been a multi-inning reliever, but he's still expected to pass the baton to a parade of relievers. Knuckleballer Matt Waldron is also expected to appear, though probably not in the typical bulk reliever capacity.
Corbin Burnes is set to make his 2026 debut for the Arizona Diamondbacks when they play the Kansas City Royals tonight in Kauffman Stadium. The righty's return from Tommy John surgery was extended by a teres major strain back in June. Burnes only made one rehab start, but he threw what was termed a bridge game, where he threw to minor leaguers in a controlled environment. He's expected to be capped at around 60 pitches tonight.

stories.headline: Arena for 76ers, Flyers to open in 2030, marks 'new era'
stories.summary: The 76ers and Flyers have unveiled renderings of their new fully privately funded arena in South Philadelphia, which is targeted to open before the WNBA season in 2030.
stories.body:
The 76ers and Flyers have unveiled renderings of their new arena on the former Spectrum site in South Philadelphia, which the organizations are calling the largest fully privately funded project in city history.

The arena is now targeted to open before the WNBA season in 2030, when Philadelphia's expansion team will begin play. The Sixers, owned by Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment (HBSE), come in as 50-50 partners with Comcast Spectacor in the new arena, after spending more than a decade as tenants.

"This is a new era for Philadelphia sports," Comcast chairman Brian Roberts said. "To build our future where Ed Snider and the Spectrum made history makes this project truly special. Working with HBSE, we are creating a world-class experience worthy of Philadelphia's incredible fans."

The Spectrum-inspired design includes more than a half-acre of outdoor gathering space, with fan plazas, food and beverage options and a large entrance staircase inspired by the steps at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

"Philly fans deserve the best arena in the world, and we are excited to partner with Comcast to deliver just that," Sixers managing partner Josh Harris said. "This privately funded arena will be the home to moments and memories that define this city for generations."

Added NBA commissioner Adam Silver: "I'm thrilled to see the first renderings of what promises to be an extraordinary home for NBA and WNBA basketball as well as many other world-class events. Beyond the incredible experience the new arena will bring to fans, I commend HBSE and Comcast for such a significant economic investment in Philadelphia."

For the Flyers, the move brings the franchise back to the grounds where it began play in 1967 and won its only two Stanley Cups.

Since taking over as Flyers governor in 2023, Dan Hilferty has also overseen a restructuring of Philadelphia's front office and made returning the franchise to consistent Stanley Cup contention a priority.

"This new arena will be a state-of-the-art home worthy of the Flyers, their fans, and the entire city," NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said. "Comcast Spectacor and HBSE's commitment to this project reflects a shared belief in Philadelphia's future and a lasting investment in the city's economic vitality."

The organizations project the arena will create nearly 15,000 jobs and generate nearly $6 billion in economic activity over the next decade, along with hundreds of millions of dollars in new tax revenue benefiting the city and the School District of Philadelphia.

stories.headline: Germany beats South Korea, rolls into World Cup quarterfinals
stories.summary: Host Germany advanced to the quarterfinals of the women's FIBA World Cup with a morale-boosting 94-56 rout of South Korea on Tuesday, and the United States learned its next opponent.
stories.body:
BERLIN -- Host Germany advanced to the quarterfinals of the women's FIBA World Cup with a morale-boosting 94-56 rout of South Korea on Tuesday, and the United States learned its next opponent.

Hungary, which beat Japan 84-63, will play the four-time defending champion U.S. on Thursday.

Germany captain Marie Gülich led her team to a quarterfinal against European champion Belgium with 19 points and five rebounds.

Every German score elicited huge cheers from the appreciative home fans at the Berlin Arena, particularly in the first half. Germany led by 17 points at halftime.

The home team has been gradually improving since losing its first group game by 30 points to Spain. Germany rebounded with a 74-58 win over Japan and followed with an 83-58 win over Mali.

Hungary eliminates Japan Réka Lelik led Hungary with 23 points and eight rebounds in a surprisingly comfortable win over Japan earlier.

Virág Takács-Kiss also had eight rebounds and added 17 points for Hungary, which will face the U.S. in the late quarterfinal slot Thursday.

"It feels incredible. It's been 40 years since we went to the quarterfinals and I still can't believe it," Lelik said.

The game was overshadowed by a serious injury to Japan shooting guard Saki Hayashi, who went off with what looked a broken right arm after an awkward fall.

Hayashi needed immediate medical attention a foul in the air from Agnes Torok with just over a minute left in the second quarter. A blue tarp was provided to give her privacy and fans responded with applause when she was led off.

Japan connected on only seven 3-pointers Tuesday. The Japanese had set a record with 20 three-pointers in a World Cup game on Friday before France broke it with 22 on Monday.

Ramu Tokashiki's two free throws drew Japan level at 34-34, but that was as close as it got. Agnes Studer responded with a 3-pointer to give Hungary a 37-34 lead at halftime.

"They hit their open shots, we missed our open shots," Japan coach Corey Gaines said.

Hungary finished 11 of 25 from beyond the arc on the first of two days off for the U.S., which qualified directly for the quarterfinals as a group winner.

"I'm excited to play the very best players in the world, the best team in the word," Lelik said of Thursday's game. "I never got the opportunity to play against them. So I'm just very excited how it's going to be. And we're going to do everything for sure. But besides that, I want us to enjoy the game."

Still two places up for grabs All the quarterfinals are scheduled for Thursday. Spain and France await the winners of Wednesday's playoffs between Italy-Australia and China-Puerto Rico, respectively.

stories.headline: Jude Bellingham takes responsibility for Real Madrid not thrashing Inter Milan: 'Two sitters'
stories.summary: Jude Bellingham admitted he missed "two sitters" as Real Madrid struggled to a 2-1 Champions League win over Inter Milan at the Bernabéu.
stories.body:
Jude Bellingham admitted he missed "two sitters" as Real Madrid struggled to a 2-1 Champions League win over Inter Milan at the Bernabéu.

Visitors Inter were the better team for much of Tuesday's game, having more possession and creating more chances, but Madrid came out on top thanks to first-half goals from Kylian Mbappé and Federico Valverde.

Midfielder Bellingham was close to grabbing a third goal before halftime, and could have added another after the break -- set up by a spectacular dribble from Brahim Díaz -- as Inter pulled a goal back through Carlos Augusto to ensure a nervous finale.

"We created so many chances again tonight, myself included, two sitters," Bellingham told CBS. "The goalkeeper [Josep Martínez] has done well to be fair, but I've just got to put the ball in the net.

"The first one was just more instinct. The second one, I just got in my own head ... It's frustrating, not so much personally, but we could have made the game easier for the team.

"In the end we're defending a one-goal lead, backs to the wall, and people will probably forget all the good things we did, because we didn't win four or five nil, and that's partly my fault."

Bellingham has been one of the standout performers for Madrid so far this season under new coach José Mourinho, with two goals and two assists in LaLiga.

- Henry backs Mbappé for Ballon, Olise over Kane

- Mourinho: Trent isn't a midfielder despite CL start

- Giggs: Utd scouted Mbappé, didn't try to sign him

The team slipped to a 1-0 defeat at Real Betis on Friday to drop their first points of the season, but returned to winning ways against Inter, with Thibaut Courtois starring in goal.

"It could have finished five or six-one to us, or it could have finished 6-6," Mourinho said. "I wouldn't say [Inter] could have won, because we created more in the crucial moments, like the 3-0 for Jude at the end of the first half.

"It was a crazy game. I don't like that kind of madness, I like being able to score five or six or seven, but having absolute control, and not needing an incredible goalkeeper."

stories.headline: Under pressure: those with the biggest questions to answer in the semis
stories.summary: Two cut-throat AFL semifinals. Two of four teams facing the end of the road. And that means a host of individuals, players and coaches are under pressure. Rohan Connolly looks at who has the biggest questions to answer.
stories.body:
Two cut-throat AFL semifinals. Two of four teams facing the end of the road. That's the equation. And that means a host of individuals, players, and coaches are ... under pressure (yep, that Queen/David Bowie classic's going through my head now, too).

Go on, put it on and click your fingers to that bassline while you read about those most under the pump on Friday and Saturday evening.

Justin Longmuir
You won't find too many better recent examples of one result so starkly changing the narrative surrounding an AFL coach than Fremantle's loss to Hawthorn last Thursday night. Longmuir and his team had done everything right this season until then. Yet the bottom line remains they now teeter on the edge of a straight sets exit at home with Longmuir copping plenty of critical flak. The Dockers' ball movement was stymied, they were inefficient, with 57 forward entries producing only five goals, and Hawthorn created space far too easily. The "lack of flexibility" accusation has also popped up again, along with more talk about costly poor starts. Fremantle lost a home final last year to Gold Coast. A third home finals defeat in a row could damage Longmuir's reputational stocks irreparably.

Jeremy Cameron
There may not be another player under as much pressure to perform on Friday night as the dual Coleman medallist, who has been goalless for a month, and five times in his last seven outings. Cameron took just one mark and had only nine disposals against Carlton last week, lacked any sort of physical presence, and was drifting up around the wing to pick up what few touches he could manage. Cameron managed two goals in Geelong's narrow Round 15 loss to Fremantle in Perth, but even then the Cats were held to the second-lowest score of their last 10 outings. Anything less this week, and there will be an awful lot of responsibility upon the likes of Shannon Neale and Patrick Dangerfield to find Cameron's missing goals.

Josh Treacy
What's that expression, one day a rooster the next a feather duster? On August 25, Fremantle's Josh Treacy was being feted as the All-Australian centre half-forward for 2026. Just over a week later, he was getting towelled up by the critics for being "destroyed" by Hawthorn key defender Josh Battle. Treacy had just four disposals, no marks and kicked just one late consolation goal. He hadn't had a kick until late in the last quarter and was accused of not attacking the contest with his usual physical presence. It doesn't get any easier this week for him, either, given that last time Fremantle met Geelong, Connor O'Sullivan held him to 2.2 from only nine disposals, picking up 16 himself, six intercept marks and a coaches' vote. Treacy needs to improve on that effort and last week's significantly.

Patrick Dangerfield
Hang on. How can the best player on the ground in last week's elimination final be under pressure the very next game he plays? Well, being the long-time acknowledged champion he is, the Brownlow medallist is always under the microscope to an extent. If "Danger" plays a blinder, Geelong will generally win. That's pressure of its own. But then there's the memory of last year. Prior to last Friday night, it was in the 2025 preliminary final against Hawthorn that Dangerfield delivered his best September performance with 31 disposals and three goals. And the following week? Unfortunately, his banged-up 35-year-old frame couldn't repeat the dose, delivering a strangely muted 10-disposal effort in the grand final loss to Brisbane. Now, 12 months older, can he back up one superlative September effort with another?

Murphy Reid
Last year's Rising Star and this year's All-Australian might be a bit of a soft target given what he's done in two seasons, that he's only recently turned 20 and last week played only his second AFL final, but Reid was one of the biggest disappointments in Fremantle's soft qualifying final performance. Whether missing the two games prior with a groin niggle has thrown him out of his stride is an interesting question, but his usually precise kicking was unusually off-target against the Hawks, and his off night was a major factor in Fremantle lacking so much of the spark the headbanded youngster has brought to the team and which had typified their season to date.

Lachie Neale
The dual Brownlow medallist was hardly the only Lion to have a poor one last week, but there's several reasons he's probably under more pressure than nearly all his teammates this week. Most obviously, given the widespread expectation that he's headed elsewhere in 2027, this could well be his final game for the club. Plus he and the other midfielders are coming off a pantsing by the Swans and, in Neale's case, Jai Serong. Even if the Lions are to get through this, Neale remains under pressure; Brisbane would face the all-conquering Hawks, before potentially the Swans again or an old September foe in Geelong, with tagger Oisin Mullin looming as another handbrake on the two-time Brownlow winner. Neale's record in finals overall is stellar, but Brisbane has seldom needed one of his best September performances more.

Matthew Nicks
OK, let's be clear, Nicks isn't going to lose his job if Adelaide can't pull an upset against Brisbane at the Gabba, even though he might have had the Crows not beaten the Bulldogs last week. But pressure? That hasn't suddenly evaporated just because a rested Adelaide beat a lesser-ranked opponent at home and gave Nicks his first finals win. The stigma of last year's straight sets elimination remains strong, the Crows won three fewer games this season and finished five spots lower on the ladder, and their record against the very best in 2026 is hardly inspiring, 2-5 against the top five, including a 52-point thumping at the hands of Saturday's opponent at the same venue. Victory this time would absolutely shore up Nicks' credentials. Another bad loss? The question marks will intensify.

Brisbane's key defenders
Saturday was a horror show for the whole Brisbane line-up, but no-one more than its defenders, and its talls in Harris Andrews, Darcy Gardiner and Ryan Lester specifically, with Sydney pair Charlie Curnow and Logan McDonald booting 11 goals between them. McDonald successfully curbed Andrews' intercepting ability and cashed in with half-a-dozen goals, and Curnow smashed Gardiner. And the equation doesn't get any easier this week with Adelaide's three-pronged tall forward set-up featuring Riley Thilthorpe, Taylor Walker and Darcy Fogarty, who StatMate tells us has kicked at least two goals in his last eight games. Ty Gallop surely is a good chance of returning at Gardiner's expense, or even second ruck Darcy Fort. But whatever selection strings coach Chris Fagan pulls, the Lions can't afford their key backs to be anywhere near that bad again.

You can read more of Rohan Connolly's work at FOOTYOLOGY.

stories.headline: Pochettino cautious about young stars for USMNT camp amid buzz around Sullivan, Hall
stories.summary: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino said that while he is happy about the potential of young players in the U.S. pool, "we need to be careful" amid the buzz around Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan and NYRB's Julian Hall.
stories.body:
United States men's national team coach Mauricio Pochettino said that while he is happy about the potential of young players in the U.S. pool, "we need to be careful" amid the buzz around Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan and Red Bull New York's Julian Hall.

The U.S. has scheduled a quartet of friendlies starting at the end of the month, starting with a match against Peru on Sept. 26, Chile on Sept. 29, Mexico on Oct. 3, and then Canada on Oct. 6. The roster will be announced on Sept. 17, with players beginning to arrive in Atlanta three days later.

As such there is much anticipation about what young players might get called up, including Sullivan and Hall.

Upon signing on for another World Cup cycle last month, Pochettino said he would be "starting from zero" in terms of building his team.

Speaking to reporters via video conference from London, Pochettino stressed he is trying to look at the potential of young players in a balanced way, and not let expectations get ahead of a player's development.

"I think we are very happy about to have all these potential good players being young, and with a possibility to perform and to play," Pochettino said.

"Only we need to be careful. We need to be careful because when you are young, of course you need to be confident, you need to have the trust in yourself, and believe that you can perform and you can do well. But the thing is it's a limit. The balance is the most important.

"And one of our responsibilities is to protect this guy because sometime if you play well and you are 17, 16 or 18 and you play well and people started to know to talk about that you are Messi or you are a big star in the world because you do some few good things. If after you are confused and you don't manage well, that can be dangerous for your career.

"And that is what we don't want. [We want] the young guys with potential being top players to provide the platform for them to evolve and to be professional, to build their career in the best way, improving every day, being humble, being careful when they talk in the media, when they talk with the teammate, when they talk with the opponent. I think respect is the most important thing and they need to be respectful. And of course we want players with talent."

Pochettino said that one goal for this cycle to further eradicate some bad habits that currently exist in the program.

Part of this the alignment of youth and professional clubs with the U.S. Soccer Federation.

The USSF recently announced a takeover of U.S. Youth Soccer.

"I think it's important when we talk about habits, it's about talking about everything, because after the player behave on the field because of this type of decision, they came from the top, he said.

"And we need to be aligned all together in our principles and all the concept that we need to improve if we want to be competitive in every single moment in our [path] until to the first team. I think we are all focused in trying to add our knowledge."

But Pochettino added that the bad habits also include players deciding not to take part competitive tournaments like the Gold Cup.

This a reference to players like Christian Pulisic who opted to sit out the 2025 Gold Cup in order to recover from a long club season.

"We were talking [about] the habit. Before it was difficult to make the roster for the World Cup one year before, because the mindset was different and say, 'Oh, if I play, I have not holidays, I cannot arrive fresh for the World Cup," Pochettino said.

"Already, with the time, you know now that is bulls--- -- sorry -- and I think it's to change this type of idea that are not right and that our experience to build mindset with the coaches, with the people in the organization, in the clubs, and of course us, and then the player that in the way that we will plan and we will do the things is the best for them, for the player, and it's going to be the best for soccer in the USA."

Pochettino added that despite the USMNT playing four games during the window, he will bring in his standard number of 26 players, including four goalkeepers.

Anything more than that would mean some players wouldn't get minutes.

"In this period of the season, we need to be careful with the player that we are going to call," he said.

"We need the players that we'll call that [they] be available to train, but also to play. And I think we consider it at the moment ,and to call 26 players with four keepers. And I think more than this is I think it's an issue because after to train, to share the minutes, I think the player that we are going to have, we want to see, we want to give the possibility to play ... with the possibility to compete. That is the idea for the next camp."

Pochettino indicated that some players who have just switched clubs, like the Middlesbrough duo of defender Max Arfsten and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter, might not be called in in order to give them more time to settle into their new surroundings.

But he indicated there would be a balance between youth and experience.

"I think we cannot bring the whole squad [with] young players because they need to have some guys with experience already competing," Pochettino said.

"But yes, we are going to do a mix ... I think experienced player with young player that can fit together and start to work on how the young kid start to manage the pressure to play in the first team."

stories.headline: Sharks premiership window nowhere near closing: Hynes
stories.summary: Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes has refuted the widely held claim the Sharks' premiership window is about to close, as the club suffers from finals wobbles and prepares to farewell some big-name stars at season's end.
stories.body:
Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes has refuted the widely held claim the Sharks' premiership window is about to close, as the club suffers from finals wobbles and prepares to farewell some big-name stars at season's end.

Since Hynes arrived at the Sharks from Storm in 2022, the club has played finals four years in a row but won only three of nine games, although they did the reach the preliminary final the last two seasons.

But at the end of 2026 they will bid goodbye to representative players Siona Katoa and centre Jesse Ramien (Cowboys), Siosifa Talakai (Perth Bears), Cameron McInnes (Super League) and Mawene Hiroti (Titans).

Balancing all that is crafty five-eighth Braydon Trindall, who returns early from a dislocated right shoulder for Saturday night's elimination final against North Queensland, has just turned 27, while rising stars like forwards Tom Hazelton, Jesse Colquhoun and damaging centre KL Iro have only played 60-odd NRL games.

"Whenever we're in this room preparing with the players we have at this club ... I'd be doing an injustice to this club and the players coming through if I said this was our only premiership window," Hynes said.

"It wouldn't be right by the younger players as that would be saying we didn't have belief in them.

"Whoever comes into this facility with a Sharks shirt on or a jersey is always going to do a great job because we've got the coaches and senior players here that make sure that standards are held.

"We've just got a good opportunity (this year) to try and win a premiership and hopefully we'll be doing that for many years to come."

First up is the Cowboys on Saturday night at Allianz Stadium with Trindall, whose nickname is 'Tricky', back in the No.6 jersey after three weeks out.

"Very keen ... it's been very tough sitting on the sidelines so very excited to be back."

Trindall spoke to the media with his shoulder heavily strapped and not knowing yet if postseason surgery is required.

"I just had to get the strength back to where it was, or near-abouts, before I did it," Trindall said.

"I've been working hard to get the mobility through it as well and it feels like it's 100%."

He knows the Cowboys forward pack headed by Jason Taumalolo, Griffin Neame, Heilum Luki and Reuben Cotter will be heading straight for the joint.

"Yep, I'm ready."

Hynes is also ready to reignite the halves partnership that was sporadic in 2022-24, but has been a regular feature for the Sharks the last two years.

"He brings more of a '7' role to the team if you will," Hynes said.

"I know I wear the No.7 -- we can both play that sort of role, but he's got an outstanding kicking game and can play on-ball a bit more which frees me up out the back to play my natural running game.

"That was our first run together out there today and it felt we were back on the bike again.

"When we're chiming in together on both sides of the field it just feels natural."

With a mediocre finals record of late, Hynes was asked which version of the Sharks needed to show up on Saturday.

"Just the best version, and all of you have seen some of the best version of the Sharks this year.

"If we bring that best version of the Sharks we're going to be hard to stop."

stories.headline: NBA offseason recap, early 2026-27 season previews by team
stories.summary: We're looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the regular season by rolling out one team profile each weekday through Sept. 18.
stories.body:
After an eventful July full of big trades, intriguing signings and the game's biggest star shocking everyone by heading East, the NBA offseason is nearly complete. And with the regular-season schedule now out, it's time to start thinking about the 2026-27 season.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for every team.

Check out the rollout schedule below, with stories added daily:

Quick links:

Free agency buzz | FA grades | Trade grades

Transactions | Schedule | More NBA coverage

Central Division

Milwaukee Bucks: Sept. 7
Key additions: Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, Caris LeVert

Key retentions: Gary Trent Jr.

Key subtractions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bobby Portis

After 13 seasons, the Giannis era ended in Milwaukee with a mega trade to the Heat -- and the 2026-27 season will mark a major shift for the rebuilding franchise.

The Bucks hired coach Taylor Jenkins to establish a culture. They added four new players from Miami, including former All-Star and Wisconsin native Tyler Herro, and selected Brayden Burries with the No. 10 pick in June.

The Bucks will enter the season with an ill-fitting mix of players and low expectations, but they have the luxury to see what sticks long term. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Bucks offseason recap/season preview

Chicago Bulls: Sept. 8
Key additions: F Caleb Wilson, G Dailyn Swain, C Nic Claxton, G Norman Powell, Tiago Splitter

Key subtractions: None

Key retentions: F Zach Collins

For years, Chicago has been seen as one of the sleeping giants of the NBA, a once-proud franchise reduced to meandering in the play-in tournament and in the middle of the lottery in recent seasons. But the Bulls got a much-needed makeover this summer and enter the 2026-27 season with a clearer direction than they've had in years.

The changes have been full-scale: Bryson Graham was hired as the team's new head of basketball operations, Tiago Splitter will patrol the sidelines as head coach, No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson is the new face of the franchise, and he'll be surrounded by some veterans like Nic Claxton and Norman Powell to help ease his transition. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Bulls offseason recap/season preview

Cleveland Cavaliers: Sept. 9
Key additions: Peyton Watson, Mario Hezonja

Key subtractions: Dean Wade, Dennis Schroder, Max Strus, Larry Nance Jr., Caris Levert, Keon Ellis

Key retentions: Donovan Mitchell, James Harden

The Cavs' failed pursuit of LeBron James this summer turned into a pivot for a younger, athletic wing, prying Watson from the Nuggets after a career-year.

Watson averaged career highs in points, rebounds, assists and steals while shooting 41% from 3 last year, and he has in recent years been one of the strongest wing defenders in the league. That makes him a strong complement next to James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, as the Cavs hope he can provide a substantial answer to the elusive fifth starter role next to their core four. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Cavaliers offseason recap/season preview

Indiana Pacers: Sept. 10

Detroit Pistons: Sept. 11

Southeast Division

Miami Heat: Aug. 31
Key additions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Klay Thompson, Bobby Portis, Tim Hardaway Jr., Nick Richards

Key retentions: Andrew Wiggins, Simone Fontecchio

Key subtractions: Tyler Herro, Norman Powell, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis

Heat president Pat Riley landed the superstar he'd been searching for since LeBron James left Miami in 2016. Antetokounmpo is in the fold, and Miami is ready to contend for another title with the two-time MVP. Antetokounmpo is just as motivated to win his second title and remind everyone that he can be the best player in the league.

In the trade, the Heat gave up key players such as Herro, Ware and Jaquez and did not bring back Powell in free agency. They landed Thompson to a two-year, $13 million deal after the four-time champion sharpshooter worked out a buyout with the Dallas Mavericks. Miami also added Portis and Hardaway, but the team is still looking to bolster the roster around Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Heat offseason recap/season preview

Washington Wizards: Sept. 1
Key additions: AJ Dybantsa, Khris Middleton, Deandre Ayton, Tre Mann

Key subtractions: Cam Whitmore, D'Angelo Russell, Jaden Hardy

Key retentions: Trae Young

The Wizards got their jump on this pivotal offseason by acquiring Trae Young and Anthony Davis last season in trades.

Those were their two big moves and then came the big prize for losing 65 games last season - winning the lottery and drafting AJ Dybantsa with the first overall pick.

Ready to start winning games this season after losing 60 or more games in each of the past three years, Washington gave Young a four-year, $212 million contract. The Wizards added veterans like Khris Middleton and Deandre Ayton to bolster the depth behind their young core featuring the likes of Dybantsa, Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George, Tre Johnson and Will Riley. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Wizards offseason recap/season preview

Charlotte Hornets: Sept. 2
Key additions: F Naz Reid, G Grayson Allen, G Dennis Schroder, F Royce O'Neale, F Dorian Finney-Smith

Key retentions: G Coby White

Key subtractions: G LaMelo Ball, F Miles Bridges, G Josh Green, G Tre Mann

After enjoying their best season in a decade, the Hornets sharply changed course with the surprising decision to trade Ball, their franchise guard, to the Timberwolves.

Given that Ball was a borderline All-Star on a max contract, Charlotte opted for a "Moneyball" approach in hopes of avoiding the perpetual mediocrity that tripped up Trae Young's Atlanta Hawks in the recent past.

With Ball and starting forward Miles Bridges moved in separate deals aimed at collecting future draft assets and improving its cap flexibility, Charlotte is now the only team that doesn't have a single player on the books for at least $25 million next season. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Hornets offseason recap/season preview

Atlanta Hawks: Sept. 3
Key additions: Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins, Kingston Flemings, Devin Carter, Ryan Nembhard, Zuby Ejiofor, Henri Veesaar

Key retentions: CJ McCollum, Jock Landale

Key subtractions: Zaccharie Risacher, Jonathan Kuminga, Gabe Vincent, Keaton Wallace

Atlanta continued to move forward from the Trae Young trade last season by being opportunistic this offseason.

The Hawks acquired Dort and Wiggins in separate trades from the Oklahoma City Thunder to add more help around emerging star Jalen Johnson. The Hawks also kept McCollum on a one-year, $21 million deal and drafted Flemings eighth overall.

Atlanta is loaded with young wings looking to take a step forward under Quin Snyder like Nickeil Alexander-Walker did last season in winning Most Improved Player. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Hawks offseason recap/season preview

Orlando Magic: Sept. 4
Key additions: C Nikola Vucevic, G Izaiyah Nelson

Key subtractions: F Moritz Wagner, G Jett Howard

Key retentions: F Jonathan Isaac, G Jevon Carter

The Magic's biggest move this offseason was hiring Sean Sweeney to replace Jamahl Mosley.

Orlando also brought Nikola Vucevic back on a one-year, $3.9 million deal since trading him in 2021 and will use his ability to score and shoot to space the floor for Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner and Desmond Bane.

The Magic blew a 3-1 lead over top-seeded Detroit in the first round of the playoffs after Wagner went down due to injury and were in desperate need of someone who can get easier baskets and make outside shots. Vucevic should help. Moe Wagner departed for Brooklyn via free agency, separating Franz from his brother for the first time in his pro career. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Magic offseason recap/season preview

Pacific Division

Los Angeles Lakers: Aug. 24
Key additions: C Walker Kessler, F Sandro Mamukelashvili, G Quentin Grimes, G Collin Sexton, F Kevon Looney, F Matisse Thybulle, G Cameron Carr

Key retentions: G Austin Reaves

Key subtractions: F LeBron James, C Deandre Ayton, G Marcus Smart, F Rui Hachimura, G Luke Kennard, C Jaxson Hayes

James informed the Lakers he would not be returning for next season on June 30. Two days later, the team transformed the roster, with Doncic squarely as the focal point.

The biggest addition -- literally and figuratively -- is 7-foot-2 center Kessler, acquired in a sign-and-trade deal with the Utah Jazz. L.A. sent two unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and pick swaps in 2028 and 2030, not to mention a four-year, $130 million contract, to acquire him.

Mamukelashvili, Grimes, Sexton, Looney and Thybulle also signed with the Lakers, and free agent Ziaire Williams and first-round pick Carr bolster the team's young prospect pool of Adou Thiero, Bronny James and Dalton Knecht.

The most important move, though, came when Reaves, coming off a career season in which he averaged 23.3 points, 4.7 rebounds and 5.5 assists per game, signed a four-year, $180 million extension.

When the dust settled, it was a dramatic roster overhaul in what could prove to be one of the most consequential summers in franchise history, with the team also being sold for the second time in 14 months, this time to venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger, who bought the Lakers from Mark Walter at a $12.5 billion valuation. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Lakers offseason recap/season preview

LA Clippers: Aug. 25
Key additions: Rui Hachimura, Keaton Wagler, Brandon Ingram (TBD), Gradey Dick (TBD)

Key retentions: Kobe Sanders, Bradley Beal

Key subtractions: Kawhi Leonard (TBD), Nicolas Batum, Bogdan Bogdanovic, John Collins

What started as a reconfiguration at the trade deadline -- acquiring Darius Garland from Cleveland for James Harden and Bennedict Mathurin from Indiana for Ivica Zubac -- turned into a complete overhaul this summer after the Clippers let Bogdan Bogdanovic, Nicolas Batum and John Collins walk.

Their biggest move, however, was trading Leonard to the Toronto Raptors for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and draft picks, but that deal is in limbo pending the investigation into alleged salary cap circumvention by the team relating to Leonard's Aspiration endorsement deal.

In the meantime, LA added Illinois guard Wagler with the No. 5 pick in the draft and signed Hachimura away from the crosstown Lakers with a two-year, $28 million deal. And in a surprise move, Bradley Beal -- after declining his $5.6 million contract option for next season in June to test free agency -- ended up re-signing on a two-year, $13.2 million deal in mid-August to stay with the Clippers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Clippers offseason recap/season preview

Golden State Warriors: Aug. 26
Key additions: Yaxel Lendeborg, Brandon Williams, Georges Niang

Key subtractions: Quinten Post, Pat Spencer

Key retentions: Draymond Green, Al Horford, Kristaps Porzingis, Gary Payton II, De'Anthony Melton

The Warriors opted for flexibility and stability over a larger shake-up around Curry. Their much-publicized recruitment of James never gained much traction.

They brought back their veteran frontcourt trio (Green, Horford, Porzingis), but kept them all on short-term maneuverable contracts. They opted for the fit of Melton over a pursuit of scoring guard Anfernee Simons. Their big addition is Lendeborg, the 23-year-old rookie wing who they will rely upon to be a high-minute, high-impact rotation player immediately.

In the bigger picture, they protected their draft pick cupboard and lined up their books to have an ocean of cap space as they peer a bit deeper into the future while their core ages. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Warriors offseason recap/season preview

Phoenix Suns: Aug. 27
Key additions: F Miles Bridges, F Koa Peat, G Luke Kennard

Key subtractions: G Grayson Allen, F Royce O'Neale

Key retentions: F Dillon Brooks, G Collin Gillespie, C Mark Williams, G Jordan Goodwin

Phoenix followed up its surprising season with a series of moves to mostly keep its team intact, with some adjustments around the margins.

The Suns re-signed Gillespie (four years, $48 million), Williams (three years, $38 million), Goodwin (three years, $19 million) and Brooks (three years, $73 million) to new deals and made a major splash by trading Allen and O'Neale to the Charlotte Hornets for Bridges. And despite not having a pick until No. 47 in the second round of the 2026 draft, Phoenix was able to acquire Arizona player Peat -- who averaged 14.1 points on 52.8% shooting as a freshman for the Wildcats and was key to their Final Four run. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Suns offseason recap/season preview

Sacramento Kings: Aug. 28

Perry, currently in the organization's power seat, is continuing a steady transition toward the younger core he has drafted. Arkansas guard and No. 7 pick Acuff is the spotlight name on a roster populated with six players in their first two NBA seasons.

But they still have notable high-minute holdovers from the past regime, including Murray, Malik Monk, LaVine and Sabonis. Perry explored trades for Monk, LaVine and Sabonis over the past year, but didn't value the proposed returns, and the three are expected to open the season in Sacramento. -- Anthony Slater

Key additions: G Ja Morant, F Jeremy Sochan

Sadly, the Blazers made far more noise this offseason with their off-court business dealings than anything they did with their roster. Although the Blazers were the only team that sat out June's draft by not making a pick, they will add two high-profile guards to a rotation that otherwise looks very similar to last season. Lillard, a franchise icon, is back from an Achilles tendon injury that sidelined him for the entire 2025-26 campaign, and Morant, a two-time All-Star, arrived in a trade that sent Grant and Murray to the Memphis Grizzlies. -- Ben Golliver

Key additions: G Darryn Peterson, C Jaxson Hayes, G Josh Okogie

Instead, the Jazz agreed to a sign-and-trade deal that sent Kessler to the Lakers in exchange for a pair of future first-round picks and two swaps.

The return was widely considered to be great value for Utah, particularly after Kessler's deal (four years, $130 million) pushed beyond the Jazz's comfort zone, but there is now a glaring need in the starting lineup alongside Jackson and Lauri Markkanen in the frontcourt. -- Tim MacMahon

Minnesota also re-signed wing Clark and guard Hyland and acquired the 6-foot-6 Evans out of Duke with the No. 33 pick in the draft.

They sent Isaiah Joe to Detroit and traded Aaron Wiggins and Lu Dort to Atlanta in separate moves, eroding their depth.

General manager Sam Presti made clear in an interview with The Oklahoman that the impression he's been given from ownership is "the savings generated this summer, and from being out of the tax the last several years, will be re-allocated to future teams."

Watson is a draft success story, rising from the 30th overall pick into one of the league's more intriguing young two-way wings. But retaining the 23-year-old would have been expensive -- via either a sky-high luxury tax bill or a salary-slashing move to get off an important veteran and generate more breathing room for a new deal.

After Wednesday's deal to send Watson to Cleveland, Denver's front office can shift its attention to escaping the salary cap's second apron. The Nuggets are currently the league's only team above it. -- Anthony Slater

GM Zach Kleiman has overhauled the roster in the past few transaction cycles, acquiring four first-round picks when he traded Desmond Bane, a few more when he dealt Jaren Jackson Jr. and none for Morant, whose departure signaled a fresh start for the Grizzlies and him.

Memphis is in a full-blown youth movement, as 21-year-old forward GG Jackson is now the longest-tenured player on the roster. The Grizzlies say they believe they have a long-term foundation in place with their last few lottery picks: center Zach Edey, small forward Cedric Coward and power forward Boozer. -- Tim MacMahon

stories.headline: Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11, joins Red Bull junior team
stories.summary: Robin Raikkonen, the 11-year-old son of 2007 Formula 1 world champion Kimi, has joined Red Bull Racing's driver development programme.
stories.body:
Robin Raikkonen, the 11-year-old son of 2007 Formula 1 world champion Kimi, has joined Red Bull Racing's driver development programme.

Robin is currently racing in go-karts -- the first step towards single seater race cars -- and has already achieved success in national and international Rotax and WSK championships.

The Raikkonen family has shared regular posts of his progress through karting via Instagram, from his very early days in junior go-karts to his participation in championship events.

"Robin has already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting," Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said.

"His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group. At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving.

"Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders. The path through motorsport is a long one, and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential.

"We strongly believe that talent can thrive when supported by the right people, the right culture and the right environment. That is what we are committed to providing Robin as he continues his development. We are very much looking forward to taking the next steps in his journey together with Robin and his family."

Red Bull's young driver programme has been one of the most successful in the paddock, paving the way for four-time world champions Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen to enter the sport.

The team recently announced that it had signed Mercedes' talent scout Gwen Lagrue to head up the programme from the start of next year, which is also when Raikkonen will join.

- Spanish Grand Prix: Everything you need to know about F1's brand-new Madring

- Alpine's Pierre Gasly sums up rollercoaster Italian GP: 'Story of my life'

- Max vs 100: When is Verstappen race, how to watch on Disney+, how it works, who's taking part?

The programme benefits from having two teams on the grid in Red Bull Racing and Racing Bulls, allowing drivers to make their F1 debut with the junior team before stepping up to the senior team.

"We are all thrilled and excited that Robin has been chosen to further his racing path as a member of the Red Bull Junior Team," Kimi Raikkonen said. "Laurent and everyone else at Red Bull have been incredibly supportive throughout all our discussions.

"They offer a compelling and comprehensive programme to develop and nurture Robin's progress over the coming years and provide him with all the experience required to develop his natural talent, which has amply been displayed in all his karting endeavours to date.

"Red Bull's Junior Team has had years of incredible success. Its alumni include Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen amongst many others. It is thus with great humility that Robin joins this illustrious programme, and he will dedicate all his efforts to warrant the trust that Red Bull is placing in him."

Aside from the drivers currently racing for Red Bull's two teams on the grid, Carlos Sainz, Alex Albon and Pierre Gasly all arrived in F1 through Red Bull's junior programme.
